scenes.name: Def Jam y Rush Artist Management
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Rick Rubin, estudiante de veintiún años de la NYU que creía que «el rap era rock», fundó Def Jam en su dormitorio produciendo «It’s Yours» de T La Rock & Jazzy Jay; Aaron Fuchs le aconsejó buscar a Russell Simmons, un promotor con carisma, hijo de un activista de los derechos civiles, que veía el hip hop como la expresión de una comunidad. Juntos lo sacaron de los parques a la radio y a MTV con un acuerdo de distribución con CBS/Columbia y una nómina que definió la nueva escuela: LL Cool J, Beastie Boys, Slick Rick, Public Enemy, EPMD. Sin radio negra, Bill Stephney trabajaba las emisoras universitarias y la «radio de la calle» de los radiocasetes; la prensa punk de la Village Voice los adoraba. Lyor Cohen, promotor de Los Ángeles, llegó a Nueva York sin trabajo, fue road manager de Run-DMC y consiguió el primer contrato de patrocinio del hip hop con Adidas al hacer que el público del Madison Square Garden alzara sus zapatillas en «My Adidas». En la sede caótica de Elizabeth Street, Faith Newman puso orden en los derechos de autor. En 1988 Rubin se fue a Def American y Cohen presidió Def Jam; en 1990 la dirigían mujeres; en 1999 Simmons vendió su parte a Universal por cien millones y extendió la marca a Phat Farm y Def Comedy Jam. El libro recuerda las acusaciones de abusos contra Simmons.

scenes.name: Beastie Boys
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Adam «Ad-Rock» Horovitz, Adam «MCA» Yauch y Mike D venían del hardcore punk del downtown; Rubin fue su primer DJ y, tras «Cooky Puss» (1983), los fichó para Def Jam: «Rock Hard» (1984). Llegaron con chándales Puma rojos queriendo ser Run-DMC; Simmons los vistió con vaqueros rotos y zapatillas sucias, su propio uniforme: «los rompemos negros y los cruzamos blancos». Abrieron la gira Like a Virgin de Madonna (1985), conquistaron al público del Apollo con Run-DMC y Licensed to Ill (1986), producido por Rubin, fue el primer disco de rap número 1 en Billboard. «(You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (to Party!)», hecha medio en broma, les llenó las primeras filas de universitarios borrachos que los espantaron.

scenes.name: LL Cool J
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: La maqueta de un chaval descarado de Queens llegó al dormitorio de Rubin: «I Need a Beat» (1984) y Radio (1985), platino, hicieron de LL Cool J la primera gran estrella solista desde Kurtis Blow y de Rubin un productor minimalista de primera. Con dieciséis años dominaba el idioma («Rock the Bells») y el escenario; su energía agresiva representaba a toda una juventud («olvidad las Oreo, comed galletas Cool J»). En Bigger and Deffer (1987) los L.A. Posse le produjeron «I Need Love», una de las primeras baladas de amor del rap, que Simmons defendió y a Rubin le rompió el corazón.

scenes.name: Houston: Rap-A-Lot, Geto Boys y la economía independiente
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: En Houston todo empezó con las batallas del Rhinestone Wrangler: K-Rino contra Ganksta N-I-P (1987), que con The South Park Psycho (1992) inventó el horrorcore. El vendedor de coches James «J. Prince» vio que las discográficas de las costas ignoraban la ciudad y fundó Rap-A-Lot (1987): los Ghetto Boys de «Car Freak» y, recompuestos, los Geto Boys de Willie D, Bushwick Bill y Scarface. La portada de We Can’t Be Stopped (1991) mostraba a Bushwick en una camilla tras pegarse un tiro en el ojo; «Mind Playing Tricks on Me», sobre «Hung Up on My Baby» de Isaac Hayes, habló de salud mental y fue de las primeras canciones sureñas oídas fuera: de abucheados en Nueva York a llenar el Madison Square Garden. Scarface, el rapero favorito de los raperos, siguió solo (The Diary, The Untouchable con «Smile» y Tupac). Ignorados por los medios, construyeron su propia economía: sellos independientes (Suave House, Swishahouse, Bigtyme, Wreckshop), la distribuidora Southwest Wholesale y tiendas en consigna, cobrando ocho o nueve dólares por disco en lugar de céntimos.

podcast.title: Absence from "Check Your Head" Production
podcast.body: Rick Rubin, a significant figure in the Beastie Boys' early career, was not present to "guide things" during the recording of *Check Your Head*, which meant the band operated with minimal external supervision. "Rick Rubin wasn't there to guide things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commercial Vision as a Producer
podcast.body: Rick Rubin is highlighted for his exceptional commercial vision in production. He possesses a deep understanding of what the audience desires and "will devour," identifying preferences for specific elements such as choruses, tempos, rhythmic basslines, and ideal song durations, often suggesting that a song should not exceed five minutes. His expertise lies in transforming an artist's creative concepts into a finished product specifically adapted to public taste. "En Rick Craving es el hombre que sabe, por ejemplo, a la gente le gustan ese tipo de coros, a la gente le gustan ese tipo de tiempos, a la gente le gustan ese tipo de vaso-rismicas, a la gente le gusta que la canción no dura más de cinco minutos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Defense of Metallica's "Death Magnetic" Sound
podcast.body: As the producer for Metallica's "Death Magnetic" album, Rick Rubin, along with the band, maintained that the album's sound was "all fine" despite widespread fan complaints and online petitions regarding its excessive compression and lack of dynamic range. "Metallica and producer Rick Rubin say hey it's all fine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Producer Role Definition
podcast.body: Rick Rubin, recognized as one of the most important producers in history, defines the work of production in a straightforward manner: "the music producer converts the artist into a product." This perspective views music, beyond its artistic value, as a product intended for consumption and sale, aiming to reach and appeal to the public without being derogatory. "el productor musical convierte el artista en producto."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Producer for Minutes to Midnight
podcast.body: Rick Rubin served as the producer for Linkin Park's third studio album, Minutes to Midnight, a project that spanned approximately 18 months of work. "Lincoln Park spent about 18 months working on their third album, this time with producer Rick Rubin."

podcast.title: Ranked Below Joe Meek by NME
podcast.body: In 2014, the English magazine NME (New Musical Express) declared Joe Meek the most important producer of all time. This significant ranking positioned Meek above prominent contemporary producers like Rick Rubin. "Por encima de Phil Spector, Gwen Cillons, George Martin o Rick Rubin."

xref.title: "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" Recording Location (April 1991)
xref.body: For the recording of "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," the Red Hot Chili Peppers moved into a historic mansion at 351 Laurel Canyon Boulevard, built in 1918. The house, with a reputation for being haunted and allegedly having secret tunnels to the nearby "Houdini Estate," was chosen by producer Rick Rubin for its isolated vibe. A Canadian company converted the basement into a recording studio. Chad Smith, however, was too unnerved by the house's atmosphere to stay there during sessions. "In April 1991, the Chili Peppers moved into a historic mansion at 351 Laurel Canyon, Boulevard that was built in 1918."

xref.title: Vivian Trimble Death (April 4, 2023) – Cancer, Age 59; Bandmate Kate Schellenbach Was Briefly in Beastie Boys
xref.body: Vivian Trimble was keyboardist for Luscious Jackson, an early 1990s New York group mixing alt-rock, rap, and pop. Their connection to the Beastie Boys ran deep: drummer Kate Schellenbach had actually been an early Beastie Boys member before producer Rick Rubin had her ousted. Luscious Jackson toured with the Beasties and became the first signing to the Beastie Boys' Grand Royal record label. Their most successful album was *Fever In Fever Out* (1996, over 500,000 copies), featuring the alt-rock radio hit "Naked Eye." Vivian left in 1998 to settle down with a family, moved to New Hampshire, and worked as a music venue booker. She was diagnosed with cancer and died April 4, 2023, age 59. "Vivian left the group in 1998 because she was tired of touring."

xref.title: Audioslave Formed After Rick Rubin Suggested Chris Cornell; Be Real of Cypress Hill Also Auditioned
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha quit Rage Against the Machine in 2000, the remaining three members tried to continue under the RATM name with a new singer. Be Real of Cypress Hill auditioned. But after some jamming, they decided they didn't want a Zack sound-alike — they wanted something new. Producer Rick Rubin suggested they talk to ex-Soundgarden singer Chris Cornell. The chemistry was immediate. They began writing as "Civilian" or "the Civilian project" but had to rename when they discovered another group was using that name. They chose Audioslave. The group was essentially Rage with a different singer, and they were productive from 2001 through 2007. "The chemistry was immediate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Audition for Rage Against the Machine – Rick Rubin's Suggestion
xref.body: After his solo album's disappointing sales, and with Rage Against the Machine's singer Zack de la Rocha having quit, producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell as a potential new vocalist for the remaining members. The chemistry between Cornell and the instrumentalists was instantaneous, leading them to write 21 songs in just 19 days. "Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell. The chemistry was so instant that they wrote 21 songs in just 19 days."

xref.title: Career Resurgence with Rick Rubin (2000s)
xref.body: In the early 2000s, Johnny Cash's career had stagnated, but a connection with producer Rick Rubin led to the concept of Cash covering contemporary songs in his unique style. This collaboration revitalized his career, turning him into an "alternative hero" and solidifying his image as "the original man in black." "But then he connected with producer Rick Rubin and came up with the idea of Cash covering contemporary songs in his own way."

xref.title: Chris Cornell Suggestion
xref.body: In 2001, producer Rick Rubin suggested the band approach Chris Cornell, noting Soundgarden wasn't reuniting and Cornell's solo work lacked traction. A meeting in May 2001 led to instant chemistry, resulting in 21 songs written over 19 days. "At some point in 2001, producer Rick Rubin said, you know, sound garden isn't getting back together. Chris Cardell's solo work is okay, but it hasn't gained him any traction. Why don't ask him if he wants to join forces?"

xref.title: Chris Cornell's Availability Post-Soundgarden
xref.body: After the dissolution of Soundgarden, Chris Cornell had not been actively involved in many projects. This made him available when producer Rick Rubin connected him with the instrumental members of Rage Against the Machine, leading to their collaboration and the formation of Audioslave. "Now Chris hadn't been doing very much since the dissolution of Soundgarden, so why not see if there was any chemistry there?"

xref.title: Evolution of Sound and Image
xref.body: Following Adam Horowitz's entry, the Beastie Boys began to fuse punk with rap and breakdancing, a popular genre in New York at the time. Rick Rubin, who joined as their DJ, further introduced hip-hop elements into their sound and influenced their image, encouraging them to dress like street rappers in matching Adidas track outfits, backward baseball caps, and chunky gold chains. "This is when the Beasties began to explore the possibilities of fusing punk with rap and break dancing, which was getting big in New York at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation from Rage Against the Machine Remnants – Producer's Suggestion
xref.body: Audioslave formed when the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) sought a new singer after Zack de la Rocha's departure. Producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell, leading to an instant creative connection and the rapid composition of 21 songs. "Rage Against the Machine had imploded... All they needed to do was find a new singer... Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation of the Band
xref.body: After Zach de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine, the remaining instrumentalists (Tom Morello, Brad Wilk, Timmy C) considered finding a new singer for Rage but were ultimately connected with Chris Cornell by producer Rick Rubin. During their first rehearsals, the immediate chemistry led to the writing of 21 songs in 19 days, including "Exploder," "Light My Way," and "Bring 'Em Back Alive." The members were committed to forming a full band, not just a one-off project, aiming for their new work to be "the best thing" they had ever done. "The first time we got together, we just jammed together and we decided, well, let's just try writing some songs. And I think the first three days of rehearsal with Chris, we wrote, exploder, light my way, and bring them back alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kate Shellenbach's Departure
xref.body: Drummer Kate Shellenbach was "forced out" of the band by Rick Rubin. She eventually left because she found Rubin to be "childish and really, really sexist." "She considered him to be childish and really, really sexist and very soon she wanted out."

xref.title: Lack of Label Supervision for "Check Your Head"
xref.body: During the creation of *Check Your Head*, the Beastie Boys experienced "almost any record company supervision," as they "d been written off by the labels, so they didn't take a lot of interest in the project." "Rick Rubin wasn't there to guide things. The dust brothers weren't there to take control, so it was just the Beastie Boys doing their Beastie Boys thing."

xref.title: Loudness Wars Controversy with "Death Magnetic"
xref.body: Metallica's 2008 album "Death Magnetic" is considered a prime example of the negative effects of the Loudness Wars, where excessive compression eliminated dynamic range. This resulted in parts of songs that should have been quieter sounding just as loud as the louder parts, and distortion was audible on many stereo systems, even at low volumes. Despite hundreds or thousands of fans disagreeing, Metallica and producer Rick Rubin stated that the album's sound was "all fine." "Death Magnetic has so much compression on it that people say that there's distortion all over it, even at the lowest volumes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Major Label Distribution
xref.body: Friends helped Wesley form The Wesley Willis Fiasco, which toured with various indie bands. His recognition grew to the extent that he secured a record deal with Rick Rubin's American Recordings, providing major label distribution for some of his material, a rare achievement for an outsider artist. "He even picked up a record deal with Rick Rubin's American recordings, which means he actually had major label distribution for some of his material."

xref.title: Rick Rubin's Influence and Kate Schellenbach's Departure
xref.body: DJ Double R, whose real name was Rick Rubin, joined the Beastie Boys and helped introduce more hip-hop into their sound. He also suggested a change in their image, encouraging them to dress like street rappers with matching Adidas track outfits, turned baseball caps, and chunky gold chains. Rubin also "kind of forced" original drummer Kate Schellenbach out of the band, as she became fed up with him, finding him "childish and really, really sexist." "He also kind of forced Kate Shellenbach out of the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rivers Cuomo's Meditation Practice (Vipassanā)
xref.body: Rivers Cuomo practices Vipassanā meditation, a Sanskrit term meaning "to see things as they are," which has been around for at least 2,500 years. He practices at least two hours a day. Producer Rick Rubin first suggested it around 2003 when Weezer was working on the Red Album. Rivers initially feared it would rob him of angst but found it enhanced his creativity and made him "10% happier." "It's called Vispasana, that's Sanskrit for to see things as they are."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Search for New Singer – Auditions and Rick Rubin's Role
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha's departure, the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine auditioned several potential vocalists, including Be-Real of Cypress Hill, but none seemed to fit. Producer Rick Rubin eventually suggested Chris Cornell, which proved to be a pivotal recommendation, leading to the formation of Audioslave. "They auditioned a bunch of people, including Be Real of Cypress Hill, but nothing really worked. Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
